messages.subject: calc.genoprob and mr vs. em
parts:
Dear Karl,
I have performed a QTL analysis using your package in a F2-population. There are two things hard to understand for me, and I allready tried to solve them on my one, but couldn't find a good explanation for me. So sorry for asking maybe easy questions. Why do I have to perform calc.genoprob first before starting scanone? what is it doing? Correcting the "real" marker infos or simulating the loci between marker? Second question is, when I have a look at my results ( attached plot), I see totally different result for marker regression (red line) and em-algorithm (black line). What is the meaning of this two contrasting peaks? This contrast is just showing up, when I first perform calc.genoprob, which leads me back to my first question. Thank you very much for this cool tool you provided and also for being so close to users in discussions.

messages.author: 963b6d84a823404f
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Re: calc.genoprob and mr vs. em
parts: Thank you very much for this hint. I even read your book in hard copy, but missed this for my problem now. But the question about the big difference with mr and em is still not totally clear for me.

See the bottom of page 79: "The jagged appearance of the LOD curve for chromosome 4 is due to the pattern of missing marker genotype data. Recall that in the marker regression method, we split the individuals into groups according to their genotype at a marker. If an individual’s genotype is missing, that individual must be omitted, as we do not know the genotype group in which it should be placed."
And in addition, is there a way to see, if this significant interval (given this nice significant signal) is a false positive? Is there a calculation to check this?

This is what the permutation test is for. Aside from that, there's no way to know.

karl

messages.author: 963b6d84a823404f
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Re: calc.genoprob and mr vs. em
parts: Sorry for posting 2 posts directly at one time. But i forgot one question. what are the best setting in calc.genoprob for step and error? Or how can I decide on my own what to set there? Does it depend on crossing sheme, marker density?

A smaller step will mean subsequent calculations are on a tighter grid. But everything will be slower and results will take up more space.

error.prob is the assumed genotyping error rate; choice depends on your particular data. You can, in principle, estimate it (see pg 36 of http://rqtl.org/tutorials/geneticmaps.pdf). You can think of it as smoothing out the LOD curves; a larger value results in more smoothing.

karl
